study.title: Send out Your light and Your truth.
study.intro: Five verses ask God for vindication, light and truth to lead the speaker back to His holy mountain and altar, ending with the same refrain of hope as Psalm 42.
study.context: Psalm 43 has no heading. It shares Psalm 42's refrain (42:5, 42:11, 43:5) and repeats 42:9's question in 43:2, so it is widely read as the third stanza of one poem; some Hebrew manuscripts join the two. Where Psalm 42 remembers the temple from far away, Psalm 43 asks to be led back to God's holy mountain, the altar and the harp. 'Ungodly nation' in verse 1 may mean an unfaithful people or a foreign one; the text does not say, and the notes do not identify it. The Scripture is loaded unchanged from the bundled BSB.
study.peopleNote: Psalm 43 has no heading and names no person. It continues the sons of Korah's Psalm 42, so their profile is relevant background but is not linked here because this psalm does not name them. Planned paintings show light, mountain, altar and harp; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Plead my case
verses.heading: A request for vindication
verses.meaning: Vindicate me, O God, and plead my case against an ungodly nation; deliver me from deceitful and unjust men. Psalm 43 opens with legal language. The speaker asks God to act as judge and advocate, defending him against unfaithful people and liars. 'Ungodly nation' could describe disloyal Israelites or foreigners; the text does not specify. The request does not ask to take revenge but for God to make the truth known and to deliver him.
verses.context: Psalm 35:1 and 23 ask God to contend and plead the speaker's cause, and Micah 7:9 trusts that God will plead the case and bring the speaker into light. Psalm 43:1 begins with that hope.
explore: Plead my case
God is asked to act as defender. The speaker trusts God's justice.
Deceitful and unjust
The opponents twist truth and justice. Deliverance means freedom from their schemes.
verses.reflect: Is there a situation where you need God to defend you rather than defending yourself?
verses.alt: A set of balance scales rests on a stone bench at a city gate.

verses.title: God of my refuge
verses.heading: Refuge and the question of rejection
verses.meaning: For You are the God of my refuge. Why have You rejected me? Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy's oppression? The speaker calls God his refuge and then asks why God seems to have rejected him. The second question repeats Psalm 42:9 almost word for word, tying the two psalms together. Faith and confusion stand side by side. The speaker keeps running to God even when God seems distant.
verses.context: Psalm 42:9 asks the same question about walking in sorrow. Psalm 88:14 also asks, 'Why, O LORD, do You reject me?' Lament holds trust and questions together.
explore: God of my refuge
God is still the place of safety. The speaker keeps that name.
Why have You rejected me?
The question names how it feels. It is brought to God, not away from Him.
verses.reflect: What do you do when God feels like both your refuge and far away?
verses.alt: A shepherd's stone hut stands on a windswept hillside under grey sky.

verses.title: Light and truth
verses.heading: Asking to be led home
verses.meaning: Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain and to the place where You dwell. The speaker asks God to send light and truth like two guides who take him by the hand. Light shows the way; truth keeps him from deception, a fitting answer to the deceitful men of verse 1. The destination is God's holy mountain, Zion, and His dwelling. Where Psalm 42 remembered from far away, this verse asks to be led back.
verses.context: Psalm 119:105 calls God's word a lamp and light, and John 8:12 records Jesus as the light of the world. Psalm 15:1 asks who may dwell on God's holy mountain.
explore: Light and truth
God's light and faithfulness act as guides. They lead the speaker home.
Your holy mountain
The destination is the place of worship. The goal is God's presence.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God's light and truth to lead you right now?
verses.alt: Two shafts of light slant across a valley toward a mountain city.

verses.title: God my greatest joy
verses.heading: The altar and the harp
verses.meaning: Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy. I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God. The verse imagines the hoped-for return. First the altar, then God Himself, then praise with the harp. The speaker calls God 'my greatest joy' or 'the gladness of my rejoicing.' The goal is not just a building but God. The harp suggests the Levitical singers' music. The double 'O God, my God' is intensely personal.
verses.context: Psalm 26:6 speaks of going around God's altar, and Psalm 33:2 calls for praise with the harp. Psalm 43:4 imagines those acts after exile from the sanctuary.
explore: My greatest joy
God Himself is the joy. The altar matters because it leads to Him.
With the harp
Music is the response to God's presence. The singer expects to sing again.
verses.reflect: What would it mean to see God Himself as your greatest joy?
verses.alt: A wooden harp leans against a stone altar with a rising wisp of incense.

verses.title: I will yet praise Him
verses.heading: The final refrain
verses.meaning: Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God. The refrain closes the poem exactly as in Psalm 42:11. After asking for light and truth and imagining the altar, the speaker still needs to remind his soul to hope. The feelings have not entirely gone. Yet the word 'yet' points forward: praise will come. The poem ends in hope, not in completed rescue.
verses.contextTitle: The end of a three-stanza poem
verses.context: Psalm 42:5 and 42:11 contain the same refrain. Romans 5:5 says that hope does not disappoint. The final repetition shows hope chosen once more.
explore: Still downcast
The question still needs asking. Faith does not pretend sorrow is gone.
I will yet praise
The poem ends looking forward. Praise is expected, even before rescue arrives.
verses.reflect: How could you choose hope today while your feelings are still catching up?
verses.alt: A sparrow sings on a temple ledge as the morning sun lights the courtyard.
